title: I know that I don't know
hookLine: the oracle calls Socrates wisest, and he decides it's because he knows he doesn't know (Plato, Apology 21)

lines: A PAUSE, THEN A CONFIDENT GUESS.
cards: In a meeting, someone asks a question. There's a small pause, then someone answers confidently, and later it turns out they were guessing. Online, everyone has a take on everything within the hour.
Even among friends, it can feel like losing to say three little words, so they rarely get said: I don't know. Today goes back, long before yesterday's prison, to the reason Socrates became Socrates.
It starts with a friend's trip to the oracle at Delphi, and a very bold question.

teach.b: It's in Plato's Apology, his version of the speech Socrates gave at his trial.

Socrates tells the jury that his friend Chaerephon, an excitable man, once went to the oracle of Apollo at Delphi and asked: is anyone wiser than Socrates? The priestess answered: no one. Socrates says this baffled him.
He knew he wasn't wise, but a god doesn't lie. So he set out to test it. He questioned a politician with a great reputation for wisdom, and found the man thought he knew a great deal, and didn't.
Socrates walked away thinking, more or less: I'm a little wiser than him in this one small way. Neither of us knows anything very fine and good, but he thinks he knows, and I don't think I know.
Then he tried the poets, who wrote beautiful things but couldn't explain them. Then the craftsmen, who really did know their crafts, but assumed that made them experts on everything else too.
So he concluded the oracle meant something humbling: human wisdom is worth little, and the wisest person is the one who knows it. Here's a surprise.
The well-known line, I know that I know nothing, isn't in Plato in those words. It's a later summary.

teach.h: HE THINKS HE KNOWS; I DON'T.
teach.b: What Socrates claims is smaller and more precise: I don't think I know what I don't know.

Showing important people what they didn't know made him enemies, and helped lead to that trial. But it also made him someone you could actually learn from. You can't learn anything you already think you know.

how: Philosophy classes often begin with Socrates' reading of the oracle, and his habit of testing what people claim to know gave its name to the Socratic method.

a wise old teacher who gives advice in person

that's a later summary. he says: I don't think I know what I don't know.

games.q: you're Socrates. the oracle has said no one is wiser than you, and you know you're not wise. what do you do?
o: accept it and start teaching as the wisest man
test it by questioning people thought to be wise
games.why: he tests it: politicians, poets, craftsmen. he decides he's wiser only in this: he doesn't think he knows what he doesn't know.

practice: Think of one thing you have a strong opinion about but haven't looked into much, and notice how sure you feel. Then ask it the way Socrates would: how do I actually know that, and what would I need to see to be sure?
Let a little space open where the certainty was; it can feel uncomfortable, even a little free.

wordCard.voice: Oracle. The Delphic oracle that called Socrates wisest, which he read to mean: the wisest person knows they don't know what they don't.

orig.note: Greek: know yourself. a saying that, tradition says, was carved at Apollo's temple at Delphi, where the oracle spoke.

carryVoice: Your line: I don't know. Three small words that take some nerve. Eighty-six days now.
